newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU finance ministers reject Santer's jobs plan.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers reject Santer's jobs plan.

text.p: To the frustration of European Commission President Jacques Santer, European Union finance ministers on Monday again rejected a proposal to spend more than $1 billion on trans-European rail and roadways to boost jobs.

EU diplomats said Santer was visibly angered by the steadfast refusal of the ministers to endorse a plan which would give a much needed jolt to the so-called TENs projects, and would probably call on them to explain their position at a summit of EU leaders in Dublin in December.
"Santer has not withdrawn (the plan) and thinks the finance ministers should explain themselves to the European Council," said one diplomat.

The reluctance of the ministers to hand over what on the surface appears to be a small sum, stems from their all-out effort to meet the Maastricht treaty's tough criteria on budgets and debt for monetary union.
Any surplus funds in the EU budget are normally returned to national governments and there is every desire to ensure that money is not spent on projects which are deemed unecessary.
The road and rail networks were an integral part of Santer's confidence pact for employment, an initiative launched earlier in the year to tackle the union's mounting jobless rate.
With unemployment widely seen as the EU's most pressing problem, there is a desire within the Commission to appear responsive to the worries of the average citizen.

The 14 priority projects, indentified by EU leaders at a summit in Essen in December 1994, include high-speed trains between Paris and Cologne and between Frankfurt and London, plus motorways in Greece, Spain and Portugal.
The extra 1.0 billion Ecus ($1.25 billion) would kick-start nine of the 14 projects, officials said, adding that Santer's request would remain on the negotiating table.
Summing up the views of many ministers, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said the extra money was not the problem behind the slow progress made towards completing the projects.
"The hold up is administrative, technical and legal," Clarke told a news conference.
"Very large resources have gone into TENs. There is no case whatsoever of altering the financial perspectives," he added.

European Commission officials hinted that a compromise plan might eventually emerge which would include the input of the European Parliament. But they were reluctant to specify the details of such a potential accord. ($1=.7980 Ecu)
